title: Personal pronouns and demonstratives

objectives.can: Recognise the independent personal pronouns and the demonstratives 'this', 'that', 'these'.

explanation.summary: Aramaic has separate words for 'I', 'you', 'he', 'we' and 'they', and for 'this' and 'these'. Because the verb already carries the subject in its ending, the personal pronouns are used mainly for emphasis, and they have a second job: a pronoun standing between a subject and its predicate can do the work of the verb 'is'.

sections.heading: The independent personal pronouns
body: The independent pronouns are separate words, unlike the pronominal suffixes that attach to nouns and prepositions. The corpus holds these forms. For the first person singular: אֲנָה. For the second person: אַנְתְּה (or אַנְתְּ) in the singular and אַנְתּוּן in the plural. For the third person singular: הוּא (masculine) and הִיא (feminine). For the third person plural: הִמּוֹ and הִמּוֹן, and also אִנּוּן, for the masculine, and אִנִּין for the feminine. For the first person plural: אֲנַחְנָא.

Two cells do not occur: there is no second person feminine singular and no second person feminine plural pronoun in the texts. Biblical Aramaic is a small body of writing, and a grammar's full table is not always found in it.

The corpus labels these words with PronType=Prs (personal), Person, Gender and Number. A first-person pronoun has no gender in the labels, because the forms for 'I' and 'we' do not change with gender.

sections.heading: Why the pronouns are used
body: A finite verb already shows its subject, so a separate pronoun adds emphasis or contrast. In Daniel 2:37 Daniel says אַנְתְּה מַלְכָּא, 'you, O king': the pronoun points to the king himself. In Daniel 3:17 the three men say אֲנַחְנָא פָלְחִין, 'we are serving', where אֲנַחְנָא names the speakers and a participle carries the action (participles have no person of their own, so there the pronoun is needed).
Pronouns are also used where there is no verb at all, and that is the next section.

sections.heading: The pronoun as 'is'
body: Aramaic needs no verb 'to be' for a plain statement of what someone or something is. A clause can simply place subject and predicate side by side, and a third person pronoun often stands between them as a link. In Daniel 2:38 Daniel tells the king אַנְתְּה הוּא רֵאשָׁה דִּי דַהֲבָא, 'you are the head of gold'. In Daniel 2:47 the king says that your God is the God of gods: אֱלָהֲכוֹן הוּא אֱלָהּ אֱלָהִין. The little word הוּא means 'is' here, not 'he'.

The corpus does not treat this use the same way everywhere. In six places it labels הוּא or הִיא as a particle (PART) instead of a pronoun (PRON), and in a few more it is labelled a demonstrative. The reader should not rely on the label: look for a pronoun between a noun phrase and another noun phrase with no verb.

sections.heading: Demonstratives: this, that, these
body: Aramaic has a near and a far set. The near set is דְּנָה (masculine singular, 'this'), דָּא (feminine singular) and אִלֵּין (plural, 'these'). The far set is דֵּךְ (masculine singular), דָּךְ (feminine singular) and אִלֵּךְ (plural), usually 'that' and 'those'. In the texts the difference is not always kept: the English edition often renders the far set with 'this' or 'these', so read the sentence.

A demonstrative follows its noun, and the noun is in the determined state: בַּיְתָה דְנָה, 'this house' (Ezra 6:15); גֻּבְרַיָּא אִלֵּךְ, 'these men' (Daniel 6:25). A demonstrative can also stand alone as a pronoun, as in עַל כָּל דְּנָה, 'concerning all this' (Daniel 7:16).
One more form occurs: דִּכֵּן, as in צַלְמָא דִּכֵּן, 'this image' (Daniel 2:31). The third person pronoun also serves as a 'that': in Daniel 2:44 מַלְכַיָּא אִנּוּן means 'those kings'.

misunderstandings: The pronoun הוּא after a subject is not always 'he'. Between two noun phrases it is the link 'is', and the clause has no verb.
Do not expect every cell of a grammar's table to be found. The second person feminine forms do not occur in these texts..
A demonstrative does not stand before its noun as in English 'this house'. It follows: בַּיְתָה דְנָה. The noun itself is determined.
The near and far demonstratives are not a firm opposition in this corpus. The labels in the analysis give the English as 'this' for both, and the context decides.

deeper.heading: Pronouns and suffixes
body: The independent pronouns and the pronominal suffixes are related: the suffix on a noun, such as the -ֵהּ of שְׁמֵהּ in Daniel 2:20, corresponds to the independent הוּא, 'he'. The suffixes have their own lesson later in this unit.

examples.analysis: אַנְתְּה is the second person masculine singular pronoun, 'you'. הוּא stands between it and the predicate רֵאשָׁה and is the link 'are': 'you are the head'. The corpus labels this הוּא as a particle, but the use is the same.

examples.analysis: אִלֵּין is the near plural demonstrative, 'these', and it stands before the noun phrase, as the first word of the speech. אִנִּין is the third person feminine plural pronoun, 'they', matching the feminine plural noun חֵיוָתָא. Here it is the link 'are' again: 'these great beasts, which are four'.
